    AI Overview
    The CDC recommends an annual flu vaccine for everyone 6 months and older, ideally by the end of October, to reduce the risk of severe illness, hospitalization, and death. Various injectable shots and a nasal spray (for ages 2-49) are available. High-dose or adjuvanted vaccines are preferred for adults 65+. 
    Key Information About Flu Shots 
    • Types: Standard shots (inactivated), high-dose (for seniors), and nasal spray (live attenuated).
    • Recommendation: Everyone 6 months and older should get vaccinated, especially those at higher risk
      .
    • Timing: Protection develops in about 2 weeks, and the vaccine is designed to cover the current season's circulating strains.
    • Where to get: Vaccines.gov can help you find locations near you.
    • Effectiveness: While it may not prevent all infections, it reduces the severity of illness and risk of complications. 
    Vaccine Options and Target Groups 
    • 6 months and older: Afluria Quadrivalent, FluLaval Quadrivalent, Fluarix Quadrivalent, Fluzone Quadrivalent.
    • 2 years and older: Flucelvax Quadrivalent.
    • 18 years and older: Flublok Quadrivalent (recombinant).
    • 2 through 49 years: FluMist Quadrivalent (nasal spray).
    • 65+ years: High-dose Fluzone, Flublok, or Fluad are preferred. 
    Side Effects
    Common, mild side effects include soreness at the injection site, fever, headache, and muscle aches, which usually resolve quickly.

    People also ask
    When is the best time to get a flu shot?
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    The best time to get a flu shot is in
    early fall, ideally by the end of October. September and October are recommended to allow immunity to build before the virus peaks, typically between December and February. While early vaccination is key, getting vaccinated later, even into winter, is still beneficial. 
    Key Timing Recommendations: 
    • Best Time: September or October.
    • Older Adults (65+): Should wait until September to avoid waning immunity, say NCOA and HistoryOfVaccines.org.
    • Children: Children needing two doses should start as soon as the vaccine is available (late summer) to allow for the recommended 4-week interval between shots, notes www.stelizabeth.com.
    • Pregnant Women: Those in their third trimester can get it earlier (early fall) to pass antibodies to their baby, notes HistoryOfVaccines.org. 
    Why This Timing? 
    • Protection Window: It takes roughly two weeks for antibodies to develop after vaccination.
    • Peak Season: Getting it by October protects you when the virus becomes most widespread.
    • Immunity Duration: The vaccine provides protection for about 6-8 months, so getting it too early (e.g., July/August) might lead to lower protection by the end of the season. 
    It is never too late to get a flu shot, and vaccination is recommended throughout the season, even into January or later.

      Side Effects. What are the side effects of the influenza vaccine?
      About this result
      Feedback
      An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
      AI Overview
      Influenza vaccine side effects are usually mild and temporary, including soreness, redness, or swelling at the injection site, headache, muscle aches, fever, and fatigue, as your immune system builds protection; these typically resolve in a couple of days. Serious reactions like severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis) are rare, but require immediate medical attention if you experience symptoms like swelling, difficulty breathing, dizziness, or hives.
       
      Common Side Effects (Usually Last 1-2 Days)
      • At the injection site: Pain, redness, swelling, or warmth. 
      • Body-wide: Low-grade fever, headache, muscle aches, fatigue, or general malaise. 
      • For children: May also include runny nose, wheezing, or vomiting. 
      Less Common/Rare Side Effects
      • Fainting (syncope): Can occur after any injection, including the flu shot.
      • Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS): A rare neurological disorder, though the exact link and risk are debated. 
      Severe Allergic Reactions (Seek Immediate Help)
      • Symptoms: Hives, swelling (face, throat, tongue), difficulty breathing, wheezing, dizziness, weakness, or a fast heartbeat. 
      • Action: Call emergency services immediately. 
      Important Considerations
      • You can't get the flu from the vaccine: The flu shot contains inactivated (killed) viruses or no virus at all, so it cannot cause the flu. 
      • Benefits outweigh risks: Mild side effects are a sign the vaccine is working, and the protection against severe flu far outweighs the temporary discomfort, note GoodRx and AFC Urgent Care.

        What are the side effects of the influenza vaccine?

        Types. What are the different types of influenza vaccines?
        About this result
        Feedback
        An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
        AI Overview
        There are several types of influenza vaccines, primarily divided by delivery (shot vs. nasal spray) and composition, including Inactivated (IIV) (standard, cell-based, high-dose, adjuvanted), Recombinant (RIV), and Live Attenuated (LAIV) (nasal spray), with options tailored by age, with high-dose/adjuvanted versions for seniors and LAIV for healthy younger adults, all protecting against circulating strains. 
        By Delivery & Composition
        • Inactivated Influenza Vaccines (IIV): These shots don't contain live viruses and come in several forms. 
          • Standard Dose: For ages 6 months and older, often egg-based. 
          • Cell-Based (ccIIV): Made in cell cultures (egg-free) for ages 6 months+. 
          • High-Dose (HD-IIV): For seniors (65+) to boost immune response, contains more antigen. 
          • Adjuvanted (aIIV): Also for seniors (65+), uses an adjuvant to enhance immunity.
        • Recombinant Influenza Vaccine (RIV): An egg-free vaccine made using recombinant DNA technology, for ages 18+. 
        • Live Attenuated Influenza Vaccine (LAIV): A nasal spray with weakened live viruses, for healthy people aged 2–49 years. 
        Key Differences
        • Age: Different vaccines are approved for different age groups (e.g., high-dose for 65+, LAIV for 2-49). 
        • Manufacturing: Some are egg-based, while cell-based and recombinant are egg-free options. 
        • Protection Level: High-dose and adjuvanted vaccines offer stronger protection for older adults. 
        • Type of Virus: Vaccines protect against two Influenza A and one or two Influenza B viruses (Trivalent vs. Quadrivalent, though 2025-2026 is Trivalent). 
        Health authorities recommend getting any age-appropriate flu vaccine to protect against seasonal flu.

          Benefits. What are the benefits of the influenza vaccine?
          Feedback
          INFLUENZA VACCINE (in floo EN zuh vak SEEN) reduces the risk of the influenza (flu). It does not treat influenza. It is still possible to get influenza after receiving this vaccine, but the symptoms may be less severe or not last as long. It works by helping your immune system learn how to fight off a future infection.

          Administration. How is the influenza vaccine administered?
          About this result
          Feedback
          An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
          AI Overview
          The influenza vaccine is typically given as a shot (intramuscular injection) into the muscle of the upper arm for most people, or the thigh for young children, but a nasal spray (Live Attenuated Influenza Vaccine) is also available for healthy, non-pregnant individuals aged 2-49. The nasal spray is administered into the nostrils using a special sprayer, while shots use a needle to deliver the vaccine into the muscle, with the site chosen based on age and body size.
           
          Shot (Injection)
          • Method: Intramuscular (IM) injection into muscle tissue. 
          • Site: The deltoid muscle in the upper arm is preferred for adults, while the thigh (vastus lateralis) is often used for infants and young children. 
          • Type: Contains inactivated (killed) virus and cannot cause the flu. 
          Nasal Spray
          • Method: Intranasal (NAS) spray, delivered into each nostril. 
          • Site: Inside the nostrils. 
          • Type: Contains weakened (attenuated) live viruses and may cause mild cold-like symptoms, but not the flu. 
          • Eligibility: For healthy, non-pregnant individuals aged 2 through 49 years. 
          Other Options
          • Jet Injector: One vaccine (Afluria) can also be given with a jet injector (a needle-free device) for adults 18-64, though needle injections are more common. 
          Key Points
          • Most people receive one dose per flu season, but children aged 6 months to 8 years may need two doses.
          • Protection develops about two weeks after vaccination.
